int. j. prod. res., 1 december 2004, vol. 42, no. 23, 4955–4974 Sequencing problem for a mixed-model assembly line in the Toyota production system S. KOTANIy*, T. ITOz and K. OHNOz The paper discusses a sequencing problem of a mixed-model assembly line in the Toyota Motor Corporation production system, which is well known as the Just-in-Time production system. Whenever a worker in the assembly line ﬁnds that he might fail to complete his operations within the work zone, he pushes a button to call an auxiliary worker who assists him in the operations. If he can complete the operations within his work zone with the help of the aux- iliary worker, the line does not stop. Otherwise, the line stops. In the Toyota production system, it is very important to keep a constant rate of usage of every part used by the assembly line. Hence, there are two goals for the sequencing problem in the Toyota production system. The paper provides a new formulation for the sequencing problem with two goals. It considers the goal of keeping the constant rate of part usage as a constraint of the sequen- cing problem, and it formulates a sequencing problem of minimizing the total line stoppage time with auxiliary workers and the constraints for keeping the constant rate of part usage. Since this problem is NP-hard and the size of the practical problems at Toyota are huge, a two-phase approximation algorithm is proposed. Numerical examples show that the proposed algorithm is eﬃcient and can ﬁnd a good suboptimal solution. 1. Introduction This paper deals with a sequencing problem of a mixed-model assembly line in the Toyota production system that is well known as the Just-in-Time (JIT) produc- tion system (Spear and Bowen 1999). It is important to level the workload on each station on the assembly line. The sequencing problem of how to level the workload has been studied by many researchers. Most researchers assume the following conditions: 1. Even if a worker cannot ﬁnish his operations within his work zone, he returns upstream to the next unit when he reaches the downstream limit of his work zone. 2. Utility work, that is the operations that the worker could not complete, is completed by a utility worker (Scholl 1995) at any time and the assembly line does not stop. Usually, the sequencing problem of how to level the workload is formulated as a problem of minimizing the total utility work. Therefore, this formulation aims to minimize not the line stoppage time of the assembly line, but the risk of stopping the assembly line. The sequencing problem of minimizing the total utility work is known as an NP-hard problem (Scholl 1995, Tsai 1995). Many algorithms such as branch-and-bound methods, mixed-integer programming, meta-heuristics and heuristics have been presented. Some papers have studied models of the assembly line with line stoppages (Xiaobo and Ohno 1994, 1997, 2000, Ohno et al. 1995). In these models, if a worker does not ﬁnish his operations within his work zone, the assembly line stops until he can complete his operations. Moreover, Celano et al. (2004) investigated a sequencing problem, starting from the mathematical formulation developed by Xiaobo and Ohno (1997), of mixed- model U-assembly lines with line stoppages. In this sequencing problem, when a worker does not complete his operations within his work zone, the line stops and he is helped by his downstream or frontal worker, who has enough free time to complete the unﬁnished operations. They analysed the inﬂuence of this help method on the total line stoppage time and proposed a genetic algorithm for minimizing the total line stoppage time. We introduce a new sequencing problem of levelling the workload on the mixed- model assembly line at Toyota Motor Corporation. In the Toyota production system, whenever a worker ﬁnds that he might fail to complete his operations within his work zone, he pushes a button on the assembly line to call an auxiliary worker who assists him in his operations. The auxiliary worker is diﬀerent from a utility worker. A group, which is a formal organization of the workplace of the assembly line, consists of about 20 workers and contains only one auxiliary worker. However, there are many cases where a foreman of the group is the auxiliary worker. The auxiliary worker for each worker is predetermined. If the worker can complete his operations within his work zone with the help of the auxiliary worker, the line does not stop. Otherwise, the line stops at the downstream limit of his station until he and his auxiliary worker complete the operations. Moreover, when the auxiliary worker is helping at another station, he cannot be called by another worker. That is, this worker cannot be helped by the auxiliary worker and the line may stop. The sequence of minimizing the total line stoppage time with auxiliary workers is important in the JIT production system and a solution of this sequencing problem cannot be obtained by algorithms that have been developed already. To our knowledge, no one has studied this sequencing problem and thus we investigate it. Moreover, it is very important to keep a constant rate of usage of every part used by the assembly line in the Toyota production system (Monden 1983). The goal of keeping the constant rate of part usage has been recognized as another goal of the sequencing problem. The ﬁrst formulation of the sequencing problem with this goal was given by Kotani (1983) and an approximation algorithm, which is called the goal-chasing method, was proposed. Several versions of this formulation have been studied and several methods for this goal have been proposed (Miltenburg 1989, Miltenburg and Sinnamon 1989, Kubiak 1993). The sequencing problems with this goal are known as NP-hard problems (Kubiak 1993). As understood from the above arguments, there are two goals for the sequencing problem in the Toyota production system. For these two goals, past papers have proposed an objective function that includes weighted sums of the objective function of each goal (Yano and Rachanadugu 1991, Bard et al. 1994, Scholl 1995). In this 4956 S. Kotani et al. Downloaded by [Memorial University of Newfoundland] at 08:51 06 March 2015

paper, however, we will establish a new formulation for the two goals. In the case that the goal of keeping the constant rate of part usage is an objective function of the sequencing problem, we can evaluate the level of keeping the constant rate of part usage after calculating the sequence. If we set the second goal as the constraints of the sequencing problem, we can obtain the sequence by predetermining the level of keeping the constant rate of part usage. We can control this level according to the conditions of the constraints. Hence, we consider the second goal as the constraints of the sequencing problem. Consequently, a sequencing problem with two goals is formulated as a new sequencing problem of minimizing the total line stoppage time with the auxiliary workers and the constraints of keeping the constant rate of part usage. Moreover, a new idea will be introduced for the second goal. In past studies, it was required to keep the constant rate of part usage at every position in the sequence. However, even if the constant rate of part usage is kept at every ﬁve positions in the sequence, any problem does not occur in real production at Toyota as stated in Section 3. On the contrary, the sequence of cars is very important to minimize the total line stoppage time. Hence, we relax the constraints of keeping the constant rate of parts usage under the conditions that any trouble would not occur in real production and try to ﬁnd a better suboptimal solution of minimizing the total line stoppage time. Since the sequencing problem of minimizing the line stoppage time is NP-hard (Xiaobo and Ohno 1997), our problem is also NP-hard, and the size of the practical problems at Toyota is huge. Then, we propose a two- phase approximation algorithm that adopts the goal-chasing method in the ﬁrst phase and adopts a simulated annealing in the second phase. It is shown by numer- ical examples that the proposed algorithm is eﬃcient and can ﬁnd a good suboptimal solution. This paper is organized as follows. The formulation of minimizing the total line stoppage time with auxiliary workers is presented in Section 2, and the formulation of keeping the constant rate of part usage is presented in Section 3. The approxima- tion algorithm is proposed in Section 4. Section 5 shows by numerical examples that the proposed algorithm is eﬃcient and can ﬁnd a good suboptimal solution. 2. Formulation of the sequencing problem with auxiliary workers 2.1. Outline of the Toyota assembly line Toyota has continuously improved the performance of assembly lines and increased worker morale. For example, the conveyor of the assembly line in the latest factory is physically divided into several processes (ﬁgure 1), and the conveyor of each process can move independently of other processes by means of work-in- process. The process is manned by the members of a certain group. This example enhances the power and responsibility of each group. Consequently, quality and productivity of the assembly line are improved (Chiba et al. 1993). The present paper deals with the assembly line at Toyota (ﬁgure 1). It outlines the Toyota assembly line that is needed in order to formulate. It made three modiﬁcations to formulate easily without spoiling the essence of the Toyota assem- bly line. These modiﬁcations are shown in the outline of the Toyota assembly line. The process of the assembly line at Toyota satisﬁes the following conditions: 1. Process consists of K stations and its conveyor moves at the constant speed. 2. Each station k(k ¼ 1, 2, . . . , K ) is manned by one worker and is conﬁned by the following two limits of his work zone: the upstream limit, where cars enter 4957 Sequencing problem for a mixed-model assembly line Downloaded by [Memorial University of Newfoundland] at 08:51 06 March 2015

the station, and the downstream limit, where cars leave the station. Therefore, the worker in station k, who is called worker k for short, must operate within his work zone. He operates on the conveyor, and after completing his opera- tions, he gets off the conveyor and returns upstream to the next car on foot. 3. Cars are launched down the process in constant intervals, called cycle time. 4. Whenever the worker ﬁnds that he might fail to complete his operation within his work zone, he pushes the button to call the auxiliary worker. Usually, he can ﬁnish his operations within his work zone with the help of the auxiliary worker. Otherwise, the line stops at the downstream limit of his station until he and his auxiliary worker can complete his operations. If a line stoppage has occurred, then launch of the next car down the process is postponed for the line stoppage time. 5. Even if a line stoppage has occurred in a certain station, the workers in the other stations continue to operate. In the Toyota assembly line, one auxiliary worker is assigned to one process and satisﬁes the following conditions: 1. He usually stands by at a certain place of the conveyor (process). For simplicity for formulation, let a certain place be the centre of the conveyor (process). 2. He is called by the ﬁrst worker who decides that he will not complete his operations within his work zone. At Toyota, the workers are trained to call him as soon as possible when the worker will fail to complete his operation within his work zone. However, the order to call him is not clear when two workers will fail to complete their operations at the almost same time. Assume that he is called by the ﬁrst worker who will reach his downstream limit of his station without ﬁnishing his operations. This assumption is reasonable to minimize the total line stoppage time. 3. While he helps a certain worker, the other workers cannot call him. 4. He goes to the station on foot, not on the conveyor. Formulation for keeping the constant rate of part usage We propose a new idea for keeping the constant rate of part usage. The following notations are used: M number of the kind of part j ( j ¼ 1, 2, . . . , M), uj number of part j needed to produce N cars of the sequence, xjn number of part j needed to produce the cars from the ﬁrst position to the nth position in the sequence. The average number of part j to produce one car of the sequence is uj/N. To keep the constant rate of part usage, it is necessary that xjn is as close to nuj=N as possible. Hence, we can adopt nuj=N  xjn   as the evaluation of keeping the constant rate of part usage. This paper considers keeping the constant rate of part usage as a constraint of the sequencing problem. That is: ð1  b jnÞnuj=N  xjn  ð1 þ bþ jnÞnuj=N for n ¼ 1, 2, . . . , N  1, ð2Þ where bþ jn and b jn are constants between 0 and 1. Next, let us show that there is no trouble in real production by this relaxation of constraint (2). The suppliers usually deliver to Toyota four times a day. At Toyota, a subsequent process pulls parts from a pre- ceding process by means of withdrawal Kanbans, described in Monden (1983), once or twice an hour. In such case that the assembly line withdraws the parts in the sequence conforming to the sequence schedule of the assembly line from the preced- ing process, the assembly line will withdraw the parts once or twice every 20 min. If the part line produces the parts according to the sequence schedule of the assembly line, then the part line can produce the parts in arbitrary order without any trouble. If the part line delivers not only to this assembly line, but also to other assembly lines, the production ordering cycle of the part line will be longer than the time interval of delivery to the assembly line. Therefore, the part line can produce the parts under the desirable conditions of the part line. Let Q be a number that is much smaller than 30. Although we keep the constant rate of part usage every Q min, there is not any trouble at the preceding processes or suppliers from the above arguments. Assuming that the cycle time is one minute, we can consider the method of keeping the constant rate of part usage every Q cars in the sequence. Approximation algorithm We have formulated the sequencing problem of minimizing the total line stop- page time with auxiliary workers and the constraints of keeping the constant rate of part usage as a sequencing problem of minimizing TLSðNÞ with constraint (3) under the given conditions tc, vc, vm, va, Lk, N and tk r . It is required to develop an eﬃcient approximation algorithm, since the size of sequencing problems at Toyota is huge. Our approximation algorithm has two phases: construction and improvement. The ﬁrst consists of a procedure for ﬁnding a feasible and good solution that would have the almost same line stoppage time at every position in its sequence in order to improve the sequence in the second phase, and it adopts the goal-chasing method. Note that the ﬁrst phase does not obtain the sequence of minimizing TLS(N) directly. After the car at the (n1)th position in the sequence has been determined, we show how to select the nth car that would minimize the line stoppage time and satisﬁes constraint (3) in the next step. Summary This paper discussed the new sequencing problem of minimizing the total line stoppage time with auxiliary workers and the constraints of keeping the constant rate of part usage in the Toyota production system. In particular, it proposed a new formulation for the goal of keeping the constant rate of part usage. That is, it set it as the constraints of the sequencing problem at not every position but Q positions in the sequence under the conditions that any trouble does not occur in real production at Toyota. Consequently, we were able to develop a good approximation algorithm. The value of Q is very important for our algorithm. If Q is very small from the conditions of the assembly line, it is better to increase Q in the second phase to 2Q or 3Q, and so on. In this case, we need to add the constraints of keeping the constant rate of part usage to the simulated annealing used in the second phase. We can ﬁnd a better suboptimal solution by these modiﬁcations of our algorithm. Moreover, Q may be other than 1, for example Q1 and Q2. In this case, let Q in the second phase be the greatest common divisor of Q1 and Q2. Hence, we need to consider carefully how to set the constraints of keeping the constant rate of part usage. Using the proposed formulation of keeping the constant rate of part usage, new sequencing problems can be considered. Our future research will investigate these problems. Appendix 1.
